===== ORIGINAL PROMPT (initial_prompt.md) =====
Build a visually stunning, fully offline iOS app called "Aura" — a
daily generative "vibe card." Native Apple stack only: SwiftUI +
SwiftData, Core Image / Metal (CIFilter compositions or a custom
Metal shader) for procedural generative art, Swift Charts for the
recap view, StoreKit 2 for local in-app purchases (no backend needed —
App Store handles receipts/entitlements locally). No accounts, no
network, no third-party SDKs — everything on-device, forever. Follow
the ios-app-factory-rules.

CONCEPT: once a day, the user answers 2-3 quick prompts (a mood
picker, one or two tap-to-select word/emoji chips, optionally the
on-device time of day). From that input plus a per-day deterministic
seed, generate a unique abstract generative-art "Aura" card — think
painterly gradient blooms, particle fields, or flow-field line art,
NOT a literal illustration — paired with a short generated caption
built from a curated local phrase bank (never a hallucinated/unsafe
LLM call — this is deterministic, on-device, and instant). The card
must look genuinely beautiful: this is the single most important
requirement in this build. If the generative output looks like
placeholder gradients or a design-101 exercise, the build has failed
its actual goal even if it compiles and passes gates.

CORE FEATURES (favor complete over broad):
1. Daily check-in flow: fast (under 10 seconds), delightful, satisfying
   micro-interactions (haptics, spring animations) on every tap. Once
   completed, locked until the next calendar day (device local time
   zone) — handle timezone travel and DST without allowing two cards
   the "same day" or skipping a day.
2. Generative card engine: a real, documented deterministic algorithm
   mapping (date seed + mood + chips) -> a reproducible but visually
   varied composition (palette, shape field, motion-blur/particle
   density). Same inputs on the same day always render the same card;
   different days must feel meaningfully different from each other,
   not like the same template recolored. This is the technical heart
   of the app — treat it with the same rigor as an algorithm module,
   not incidental UI.
3. Collection & streaks: a scrollable archive/grid of past cards
   (like a photo grid), a streak counter, and a "your Aura over time"
   trend view (mood distribution via Swift Charts).
4. Monthly/seasonal "Wrapped": after each calendar month, generate a
   shareable recap — a short animated sequence or a single composite
   poster of that month's dominant palette/mood story (Spotify-Wrapped
   style). This is a primary viral surface — must render as a
   beautiful, portrait (9:16) export.
5. Share export: every single card AND the monthly Wrapped must export
   as a high-resolution image (and ideally a short looping video/Live
   Photo-style clip of the generative animation) sized correctly for
   Instagram/TikTok Stories (1080x1920), via the native share sheet.
   A small, tasteful, dismissible-only-via-purchase watermark on free
   exports is the monetization hook (see below) — it must never be so
   intrusive it kills the shareability that drives virality.
6. Monetization (StoreKit 2, local only): one non-consumable "Aura+"
   unlock via native IAP removing the export watermark and unlocking
   extra palette themes + the ability to regenerate a card once per
   day if unsatisfied (free tier: no regeneration). Handle purchase,
   restore purchases, and the Simulator's inability to complete real
   StoreKit transactions honestly — use a local StoreKit configuration
   file for Simulator testing and say so explicitly, don't fake a
   purchase succeeding without going through StoreKit's real API.
7. Widget: home-screen widget showing today's card once generated, or
   an inviting "your Aura is waiting" state before check-in.
8. Notifications (local only, opt-in): a gentle daily reminder if the
   user hasn't checked in yet, respecting Focus/Do Not Disturb norms
   and permission denial gracefully.

PRIORITIES, in order: (a) the generative art must be genuinely
beautiful and varied — treat this as a design/craft problem, iterate
on the actual visual output, not just "does it render"; (b) the
deterministic seeding algorithm must be correct and tested (same
inputs -> same card, always); (c) the share-export pipeline must
produce real, correctly-sized, good-looking image/video files, not a
plain screenshot of the UI. Seed a "demo history" toggle with 30+ days
of varied past cards so the archive/Wrapped/trend screens are never
empty on first review. Provide a clear way to run it in the iOS
Simulator via Xcode, and honestly flag anything StoreKit-transaction-
related that cannot be fully verified without a real device/sandbox
account.

===== PHASE PLAYBOOK (editable phase_rules.json) =====
Global app-build rules:
- Prefer a smaller finished app over a larger half-built app.
- Every generated app must have real user-visible behavior, not only placeholder screens.
- For iOS apps, default to SwiftUI, deterministic local state first, Apple system frameworks, and no third-party package unless it materially reduces risk.
- Every screen needs empty, loading, success, and error states when the workflow can reach those states.
- No two text or control elements may visually overlap, collide, or clip each other. Labels never sit on top of values; values never stack into each other. When elements are positioned by a data value (times on a timeline, points on an axis), enforce a minimum gap and de-clutter (offset, group, collapse, or drop a colliding label) — overlapping text is a broken screen.
- The interface must never claim an outcome that has not happened: show Saved/Deleted/Sent/Synced/Unlocked only after it is truly confirmed, never a success state shown unconditionally. No sample or placeholder data shown as if it were the user's real data.
- Implement the design spec's tokens as one SwiftUI theme file (e.g. Theme.swift with type, spacing, and color definitions) and reference it everywhere; never scatter font/size/color literals through views.
- Every generated app must fully support dark mode: semantic color roles with explicit light and dark values, verified in both appearances.
- Empty states are designed content (icon + one-line explanation + the action that fills the screen), never a blank view or bare 'No data' text.
- No default unstyled List, Form, or navigation chrome where the design spec calls for custom rows, cards, or backgrounds; the built UI must match the spec.
- Treat accessibility, privacy, persistence, and testing as product requirements, not polish.
- Do not declare the app done until build verification and the final review agree on what works and what remains limited.

Phase rules:
- Preserve the user's original prompt before interpreting it.
- Convert the prompt into hard requirements, non-goals, output shape, quality bar, and decision rules.
- Resolve conflicts by naming the assumption, not by silently changing the assignment.

Required output:
- Original prompt excerpt or full prompt reference.
- Hard requirements.
- Non-goals.
- Production-readiness definition.
- Decision rules for later phases.
- A NUMBERED list of testable requirements extracted from the user's prompt — each one verifiable by using the app.

Acceptance checks before consensus:
- A later phase can tell whether it is violating the user's prompt.
- Multi-app quantity/category requirements are explicit.
- Production-ready means more than a prototype or spec.
- Every promise in the original prompt maps to a numbered requirement; nothing is silently dropped.


===== RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE (curated IOS reference — use it, don't restate it) =====

----- Common Pitfalls -----
# Common iOS & SwiftUI Pitfalls: Symptoms and Fixes

Reference for building iPhone apps on **iOS 17+ / Swift 5.9+** (validated against Xcode 26 / Swift 6). Each entry is **symptom → fix** with compilable, idiomatic code. First-party frameworks only; zero third-party dependencies.

---

## 0. Fast rules (read first)

- Prefer `@Observable` (Observation framework, iOS 17+) over `ObservableObject`/`@Published` for new view models.
- All UI mutation happens on the main actor. Never call SwiftUI/UIKit off-main.
- `Task {}` inherits the enclosing actor and priority; `Task.detached {}` inherits neither. Know which you want.
- A view's `body` is a pure function of its inputs. It can run many times per second — keep it cheap and side-effect-free.
- Every `ForEach` element needs a **stable** identity. Never key on array index for mutable data.
- `@State` is for view-local, view-owned, transient state — nothing else.
- When generating a project headlessly, the `.pbxproj`/target membership, bundle id, and signing config matter as much as the Swift code. A perfect source file that isn't in the target does not compile.

---

## 1. Main-thread / UI updates

### 1.1 Mutating UI state from a background thread

**Symptom:** Purple runtime warning "Publishing changes from background threads is not allowed"; UI updates late, flickers, or crashes; `_dispatch_assert_queue_fail`.

**Cause:** State that drives the UI is written from a background queue (e.g. a `URLSession` completion handler, a `DispatchQueue.global` block, a C callback).

**Fix — hop to the main actor before touching UI state:**

```swift
// WRONG: completion handler runs on a background thread
URLSession.shared.dataTask(with: url) { data, _, _ in
    self.items = decode(data)   // ❌ background-thread UI mutation
}.resume()

// RIGHT: async/await keeps you on the caller's actor
@MainActor
func load() async throws {
    let (data, _) = try await URLSession.shared.data(from: url)
    items = try JSONDecoder().decode([Item].self, from: data) // ✅ on main
}
```

If you're stuck with a callback API, bridge explicitly:

```swift
someLegacyAPI { result in
    Task { @MainActor in
        self.items = result   // ✅ explicit hop to main
    }
}
```

- Do **not** sprinkle `DispatchQueue.main.async` everywhere as a superstition. Model the actor boundary once (usually `@MainActor` on the view model) and let the compiler enforce it.
- `@Observable` classes are **not** implicitly main-actor. Mark the type `@MainActor` if it owns UI state.

### 1.2 Blocking the main thread with sync work

**Symptom:** Frozen UI, dropped frames, watchdog `0x8badf00d` termination on launch, a spinner that never spins.

**Cause:** File I/O, JSON decoding of large payloads, image resizing, or `Data(contentsOf:)` on the main thread.

**Fix — move CPU/IO work off-main, then return the result. Prefer the async `byPreparingThumbnail` API, which does the decode/resize off the main thread and never blocks:**

```swift
@MainActor
func thumbnail(from data: Data) async -> UIImage? {
    guard let image = UIImage(data: data) else { return nil }
    // Decode + downsample happen off-main; returns on the calling actor.
    return await image.byPreparingThumbnail(of: CGSize(width: 200, height: 200))
}
```

- Never use `Thread.sleep`, semaphores, or `DispatchGroup.wait()` on the main thread.
- Never do synchronous networking (`Data(contentsOf: remoteURL)`) — it blocks and is not cancellable.

---

## 2. async/await, Task, and @MainActor

### 2.1 `Task {}` vs `Task.detached {}`

**Symptom:** Either an unexpected main-thread hop, or a data-race warning, depending on which you picked by accident.

**Rule:**
- `Task {}` **inherits** the current actor, priority, and task-local values. Inside a `@MainActor` type, its body runs on the main actor.
- `Task.detached {}` inherits **nothing** — no actor, no priority, no task-locals. Use it only for genuinely independent background work (and reach for it rarely; a `nonisolated` async function is usually the cleaner way to get off-main).

```swift
@MainActor
final class FeedModel {
    var state: LoadState = .idle
    let api: API

    init(api: API) { self.api = api }

    func refresh() {
        Task {                    // ✅ runs on MainActor; safe to touch state
            state = .loading
            let feed = (try? await api.fetch()) ?? []
            state = .loaded(feed)
        }
    }
}
```

- Prefer structured concurrency (`async let`, `TaskGroup`) over spawning unstructured `Task {}` when results must be awaited.

### 2.2 Fire-and-forget tasks that outlive the view

**Symptom:** "Modifying state during view update" logs; work continues after the view disappears; wasted network calls; crashes touching a deallocated model.

**Fix — bind the task lifetime to the view with `.task`:**

```swift
struct FeedView: View {
    @State private var model = FeedModel(api: .live)

    var body: some View {
        List(model.items) { ItemRow(item: $0) }
            .task { await model.load() }   // ✅ auto-cancelled on disappear
    }
}
```

- `.task(id:)` re-runs when `id` changes and cancels the previous run — the correct way to react to a changing parameter (e.g. a selected user id).
- A bare `Task {}` in `onAppear` is **not** cancelled automatically. Only use it when you truly want a lifetime detached from the view, and store/cancel it yourself.

### 2.3 Ignoring cancellation

**Symptom:** A search-as-you-type view fires a request per keystroke and races; stale results overwrite fresh ones.

**Fix — debounce inside `.task(id:)`, which cancels the previous run on each new keystroke:**

```swift
.task(id: query) {
    do {
        try await Task.sleep(for: .milliseconds(300)) // debounce; throws on cancel
        results = try await search(query)
    } catch {
        // CancellationError from a superseded keystroke, or a search failure.
        // Either way, don't overwrite fresh results with stale/empty data.
    }
}
```

Now my read on this, wearing the skeptic hat.

The single biggest risk in this whole build is that "beautiful" is unfalsifiable by any gate we normally run. A build can compile, pass SwiftData tests, pass StoreKit sandbox flows, and still render something that looks like a gradient picker demo from a SwiftUI tutorial. Nothing in our normal verification toolchain (unit tests, build success, simulator boot) catches "this looks like a design-101 exercise." If later phases don't bake in an explicit visual-review checkpoint — someone or something actually looking at rendered card output at multiple seed values side by side and judging variety and polish — this requirement will get quietly satisfied on a technicality. I'd treat "renders and compiles" as necessary but nowhere near sufficient, and I'd insist the production-readiness definition explicitly names a visual QA step with rendered screenshots across at least 5-10 different mood/chip/date combinations before anyone calls this done.

Second risk: the determinism requirement and the "regenerate once per day" paid feature are in direct tension, and the prompt doesn't resolve it. If regeneration must still be deterministic-with-same-inputs, then "regenerate" needs its own seed dimension (e.g., a regeneration counter or nonce folded into the hash) that isn't just "date + mood + chips," otherwise regenerating produces the identical card and the paid feature is a no-op — a real functional bug that would only show up if someone actually taps the regenerate button and compares. This needs to be named as an explicit assumption: regeneration introduces an additional seed component, and the "same inputs same day" determinism guarantee applies only to the base card, not to post-regeneration state. If a later phase doesn't write this down, someone will build regenerate as literally re-running generation with the same seed and ship something that visibly does nothing.

Third, the date/timezone requirement is exactly the kind of thing that sounds simple and is actually a notorious source of real bugs: DST transitions, travel across timezones mid-day, a device clock changed manually, midnight boundary races if the app is generating right at 23:59:59. "Locked until next calendar day, device local time" needs a concrete testable definition — which calendar, which timezone snapshot (at check-in time vs. at query time), and explicit handling for backward clock changes (does going back in time re-unlock today's check-in? it must not). This is a place where "handle it" is not a requirement, it's a wish, and I'd want a numbered test that includes: simulate a manual clock change backward across a day boundary, and confirm the app does not allow a second check-in for the day already recorded.

Fourth, on "demo history" — the prompt calls for 30+ days of seeded past data so the archive/Wrapped screens aren't empty on first review. This is good, but it's also a common source of a very specific dishonesty pattern: an app that shows synthetic demo data indiscriminately blended with real data, or that fails to visually distinguish demo mode from the user's real streak, would violate the factory rule that no placeholder data may be presented as if it's real. I want the contract to require that demo history is an explicit, clearly labeled, toggle-controlled state — on by default only for first-review purposes — and that turning it off does not corrupt or merge with genuine future check-ins (i.e., demo-seeded days shouldn't count toward a real streak once the user starts actually using the app, or if they do count, that's a named decision, not an accident).

Fifth, StoreKit honesty: the prompt explicitly demands we not fake a purchase succeeding without going through the real API, and explicitly acknowledges the Simulator can't complete real transactions. That means the production-readiness bar for this feature is capped — full purchase completion literally cannot be verified in Simulator, only initiation, the local StoreKit configuration file's product listing, and restore-purchases logic against that config. Any later phase's "verified" claim about IAP must say exactly this, not silently claim full purchase verification. I'd also flag: restore purchases needs a defined behavior when there's nothing to restore (a real state, not a crash or silent no-op with no feedback), and denial/interruption/failed-transaction paths need explicit handling, not just the happy path.

Sixth, share export at 1080x1920 correctly sized and "not a screenshot of the UI" is a testable, falsifiable claim — the later build phase should produce an actual exported file we can inspect (pixel dimensions, aspect ratio, that it's a rendered composition and not a captured screen including status bar/chrome). This is one of the few places in this whole spec where we can write an objective pass/fail test, so it should be exploited as such. Non-goals worth naming explicitly, since the prompt is generous but not unlimited: no accounts, no network calls of any kind (including analytics/crash reporting SDKs, which are third-party and would violate "no third-party SDKs"), no cloud sync/backup beyond whatever SwiftData+CloudKit the user's own iCloud might do by default (this should probably be explicitly disabled unless the user asks, since "no accounts, no network" argues for local-only persistence, no iCloud mirroring). Also worth flagging: "short looping video/Live Photo-style clip" is marked "ideally" — that's a soft requirement, and I'd treat static high-res image export as the hard requirement and animated/video export as a stretch goal that shouldn't block completion, otherwise scope creep on video encoding (a genuinely hard technical problem with Metal/AVFoundation) could sink the whole build trying to chase a "nice to have."

For the numbered testable requirements the phase output needs, here's my pass, framed so any later phase can check pass/fail directly against the running app:

1. A user can complete a daily check-in (mood + 1-2 chips, optional time-of-day) in under 10 seconds of interaction time, with haptic and spring-animation feedback on each tap.
2. After completing today's check-in, the check-in flow is locked (no second card generated) until the device's calendar day changes, correctly across a DST transition and across a timezone change (e.g., flight landing in a new zone), and a backward clock change does not re-unlock or duplicate today's entry.
3. Given the same date seed + mood + chip selection, the generated card (palette, shape field, particle/motion density) is pixel-for-pixel or parameter-for-parameter identical on repeated runs; given a different date, mood, or chip combination, the card is visibly and meaningfully different, not a recolor of the same template — verifiable by rendering and visually comparing at least 8-10 distinct combinations.
4. The generated card is judged by a human/visual review step (not just "did it render") against the bar of "genuinely beautiful," with a named process for that judgment, not merely absence of crashes.
5. The archive/grid view shows past cards, a streak counter reflects consecutive real check-in days correctly (including across the timezone/DST edge cases in #2), and the mood-distribution trend view renders via Swift Charts with real (or clearly labeled demo) data.
6. A "demo history" toggle populates 30+ days of varied, clearly-labeled synthetic past cards so archive/streak/trend/Wrapped screens are non-empty on first launch, and disabling it does not silently blend fabricated days into the user's real streak count.
7. After a calendar month completes (or on-demand for demo data), a monthly "Wrapped" recap is generated and exports as a portrait 9:16 composite poster (and/or short animated sequence) reflecting that month's actual dominant mood/palette data.
8. Every individual card and the Wrapped recap can be exported via the native share sheet as an actual image file at 1080x1920, verifiably not a raw UI screenshot (no status bar/chrome, correct pixel dimensions).
9. Free-tier exports carry a small, dismissible-only-via-purchase watermark that does not obscure the card's visual center or caption.
10. The non-consumable "Aura+" IAP, when purchased via the local StoreKit configuration file in Simulator, removes the watermark, unlocks additional palette themes, and enables one regeneration per day; regeneration produces a card visually distinct from the original for the same date/mood/chips (i.e., regeneration uses an additional seed input, not a no-op re-run).
11. Restore Purchases correctly restores the Aura+ entitlement when applicable and gives explicit, honest feedback when there is nothing to restore — no fabricated success state.
12. A home screen widget shows today's completed card once generated, or a distinct "your Aura is waiting" invitation state before check-in — never a stale or blank widget.
13. Opt-in local notifications remind the user once daily if they haven't checked in, and permission denial is handled gracefully (no repeated prompting, no crash, no silent assumption of consent).
14. No network calls occur anywhere in the app (verifiable via network conditioner / no outbound traffic), and no third-party SDK is present in the dependency graph.

My biggest objection to the plan as written, going into later phases: if the "beautiful" bar and the demo-data honesty bar aren't given an explicit verification mechanism now, they'll get rubber-stamped by default at the build-verification phase because everything else (compiles, passes unit tests) is comparatively easy to check mechanically, and the hard-to-verify aesthetic/data-honesty requirements will quietly become "trust me." That's the failure mode I'd want the group to commit to guarding against before we move on.
